title: Capstone Project
blurb: Tests how to scope a capstone so every lifecycle stage gets a real version, why the dataset isn't handed over, writing a problem statement, splitting effort across the lifecycle, explaining results to a non-technical stakeholder, and what the predictive-maintenance example found.

refLinks.label: §37.2.1 Scoping: The Skill Most Learners Underrate

ideas.title: Deployment and monitoring are part of the job

refLinks.label: §37.2.3 Deployment and Monitoring Are Not Optional Extensions
§37.2.2 Why a Capstone Deliberately Doesn’t Specify a Dataset

questions.prompt: What does the chapter call the most common way capstones fail?
options: Using too few features in the final model
Scope, either too ambitious or too safe
Choosing the wrong model family for the data
Running out of compute before training finishes
questions.explanation: The chapter says the most common failure isn't a modelling mistake. Projects that try everything do every stage shallowly and cut deployment first. Projects on clean, famous datasets skip the hard parts.

refLinks.label: §37.2.1 Scoping: The Skill Most Learners Underrate

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter warn against a capstone on a clean, famous, heavily solved dataset?
options: It skips data cleaning and problem framing, so it shows only that .fit() can be called.
Famous datasets have licences that forbid their use in a portfolio project.
Models on famous datasets always overfit, because their test sets have long since leaked online.
Famous datasets are too large to train on in the time a capstone allows.
questions.explanation: The "too safe" failure avoids the hardest, most realistic parts of the job. Licences, leakage and size are not the chapter's concern here.

refLinks.label: §37.2.1 Scoping: The Skill Most Learners Underrate

questions.prompt: Breadth against depth. What does the chapter prefer?
options: Touching every chapter lightly, since breadth shows the most skill
Going deep on 8 to 10 well-chosen techniques while handling the rest competently
Going deep on a single technique and skipping the other lifecycle stages
Whatever the stakeholder asks for, since depth and breadth matter equally in a capstone
questions.explanation: Light coverage of everything shows breadth but nothing deeply. Depth on the right techniques shows the judgement a real project needs: knowing where the hard problem is and spending time there.

questions.prompt: A learner plans a capstone: churn prediction, deployment, a full monitoring dashboard, automated retraining, and a RAG chatbot over support tickets, alone, in six weeks. What is the chapter's advice?
options: Cut it so every lifecycle stage gets a real, if modest, version.
Drop the churn model and keep only the chatbot, since GenAI is more impressive.
Drop deployment and monitoring, since modelling is the real work.
Keep the plan, since ambitious projects make the strongest portfolio pieces.
questions.explanation: This is the "too ambitious" failure, a team's quarter rather than a solo project. Under pressure, deployment and monitoring get cut first, which are the stages the chapter says not to cut. GenAI belongs only where it fits naturally.

refLinks.label: §37.2.1 Scoping: The Skill Most Learners Underrate

questions.prompt: In Procedure 37.2's effort split, which stage does the chapter call usually the real bottleneck?
options: The write-up and the final presentation
Modelling and evaluation
Cleaning and feature engineering
Deployment
questions.explanation: Cleaning and feature engineering get 25% and the note "usually the real bottleneck". Modelling also gets 25%, with the note that it is often over-invested relative to its payoff.

questions.prompt: A solo capstone has a 60-hour budget. Using Procedure 37.2's split, how many hours go to deployment?
questions.explanation: Deployment gets 20%, and 0.20 × 60 = 12 hours. Monitoring gets another 10%, or 6 hours. Both are marked "do not cut".

options: Deploying too early, before the model has been tuned against a strong baseline
Spending too long on the write-up and leaving too little time to clean the data properly first
Monitoring too much, so alerts fire on every small change in the data
Spending most of the time on model architecture, then running out of time to deploy and monitor
questions.explanation: The procedure names spending 70% of the time on architecture as the trap. A modest model that is deployed and monitored shows more of the book's premise than a tuned model left in a notebook.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter treat deployment and monitoring as required, not as polish?
options: A validation metric shows only half the lifecycle.
SageMaker requires every model to be deployed before it is registered.
Monitoring is needed to compute the validation metric in the first place.
Deployment is the only stage employers ask about in interviews.
questions.explanation: The chapter says a model that exists only in a notebook hasn't been built to production standard. The AWS callout says a locally run capstone is enough, so SageMaker is optional.

refLinks.label: §37.2.3 Deployment and Monitoring Are Not Optional Extensions

questions.prompt: Which elements does Procedure 37.1 require in a problem statement? Select all that apply.
options: The business question the model informs
A measurable success metric and threshold, justified by error costs
What is out of scope
Who uses the output, and how
The model architecture to be used
questions.explanation: The four elements are business question, success criteria, out of scope and stakeholder. The model is chosen later, from measurement, which is the worked example's lesson.

questions.prompt: Why is "build a model to predict pump failure" not a problem statement?
options: It is too short. Problem statements must run to at least a page.
It uses the word "model", which belongs only in the technical write-up.
It names a specific asset, and problem statements must stay general.
It's a task, with no why and no bar for good enough.
questions.explanation: Procedure 37.1's common mistake. A business question says what decision the model informs, and success criteria say what threshold is good enough given the costs of each error.

questions.prompt: Why does the capstone deliberately not hand you a dataset?
options: Judging whether messy real data can answer the question is part of the job.
Choosing a dataset is a legal step that the book can't do for you.
The book's datasets are all used up by earlier chapters' examples.
Any dataset is fine, so the choice doesn't affect the project.
questions.explanation: Earlier chapters used curated data to keep one lesson clean. Real practitioners get whatever a customer's systems produce, and selecting and judging the data is a core skill.

refLinks.label: §37.2.2 Why a Capstone Deliberately Doesn’t Specify a Dataset

questions.prompt: What does Procedure 37.3 say not to lead with when presenting to a non-technical stakeholder?
options: What data it was trained on
What the model does, in one sentence
What the model doesn't do
A raw metric like ROC-AUC
questions.explanation: A stakeholder has no feel for an AUC of 0.87. Translate it into what it means for their decision. The other three are parts of the procedure's template.

questions.prompt: A model's precision is 0.25. How many false alarms does it raise per correct flag? Use (1 − precision) / precision.
questions.explanation: 0.75 / 0.25 = 3. Of every four flags, one is a real failure and three are false alarms. That is the kind of translation Procedure 37.3 asks for.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best follows Procedure 37.3 for a model with recall 0.79 and about 3 false alarms per correct flag?
options: It catches about 4 in 5 real failures, with about 3 unneeded inspections per catch.
It has a recall of 0.79 and a precision of 0.26 on the held-out test set, with a class-balanced loss.
It reached a ROC-AUC well above the 0.5 that a random model gets.
It is 79% accurate, so it is right about four times in every five.
questions.explanation: The procedure turns metrics into decision terms. The second option is raw metrics. The third confuses recall with accuracy, which would mislead. The fourth leads with AUC, the procedure's common mistake.

questions.prompt: When does the chapter say a GenAI extension belongs in a capstone?
options: Only when the classical model performs badly
When the problem is a natural fit, such as drafting ticket replies with RAG
Always, since it shows the full breadth of the book
Never, since GenAI is out of scope for a data science capstone
questions.explanation: Most tabular problems have no natural place for prompts, retrieval or agents, and forcing one in is a scoping mistake. A rigorous classical capstone that nails deployment and monitoring is complete on its own.

questions.prompt: The worked example has 193 failures in 2,000 pump readings. What is the base failure rate, as a percentage? Give two decimal places.
questions.explanation: 193 / 2,000 = 0.0965, or 9.65%. That is a realistic class imbalance, which is why the models use class_weight="balanced".

questions.prompt: Which model did the worked example favour, and why?
options: The random forest, which had the higher precision and so raised fewer false alarms per correct flag.
The random forest, because ensembles are generally the stronger choice.
Neither, because the two were within cross-validation noise of each other.
Logistic regression, which caught 38 of 48 failures to the forest's 12.
questions.explanation: LR's test recall was 0.79 against 0.25. Missed failures are far costlier than extra inspections here, so 2.89 false alarms per correct flag against 2.50 is an easy trade. The CV gap of about 0.41 dwarfs the standard deviations of 0.06 and 0.04.

questions.prompt: In the monitoring check, temperature PSI was 0.4704 and the vibration control was 0.0482. What does that show?
options: Both features drifted, since any PSI above zero is a significant shift.
The check flagged the real +6° shift and correctly left the no-drift control alone.
Neither drifted, since both PSI values are below 1.
Vibration drifted more than temperature, since its readings had missing values.
questions.explanation: 0.4704 is past the 0.25 "major shift" line. 0.0482 is under 0.1, no significant shift. A no-drift control shows the check doesn't fire on noise.

questions.prompt: What does the chapter's mental model say the worked example's main finding was?
options: PSI is the most important metric in any capstone, more than recall.
Synthetic data always favours simple models, so the result says nothing about real data.
The "obviously stronger" model was wrong for this cost-asymmetric problem, which only measuring both showed.
Random forests can't handle missing values, so imputation broke them.
questions.explanation: The finding wasn't a new technique but the discovery, by measuring, that the reflexive choice was wrong here. Both pipelines imputed missing values first. The chapter makes no claim that synthetic data always favours simple models.

bookExercises.prompt: List the four required elements of a capstone problem statement (Procedure 37.1) and state which one is missing from "build a model to predict pump failure."
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The four elements: Business Question, Success Criteria, Out of Scope, Stakeholder. "Build a model to predict pump failure" states a task, not a business question. It's missing all four elements: why the prediction matters (business question, properly framed), what counts as good enough (success criteria with a cost-justified threshold), what's deliberately excluded (out of scope), and who uses the output (stakeholder).

bookExercises.prompt: State Procedure 37.2's two lifecycle stages most commonly cut under time pressure, and explain in one sentence why that's the wrong stage to cut, per this chapter's Motivation.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Deployment and monitoring. Per Motivation, cutting these under time pressure means the stages that most distinguish a data scientist from a Kaggle-style notebook exercise get dropped first: exactly the stages that demonstrate a model was built to production standard rather than existing only as a validation-set metric in a notebook cell.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 37.4's measured results (LR: 79.2% failures caught; RF: 25.0% failures caught), explain why the cross-validation standard deviations (0.0617 and 0.0402) are relevant evidence that this gap is real signal and not noise, and connect this to Chapter 13's cross-validation chapter.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The cross-validation standard deviations (0.0617 for LR, 0.0402 for RF) describe the spread of recall scores across the 5 folds for each model individually. Both are small relative to the 0.4069 gap between the two means (0.7241 vs. 0.3172). If the gap between models were smaller than roughly the sum of their standard deviations, it would be plausible that fold-to-fold noise alone explains the difference. Here the gap is roughly 6-7x the larger of the two standard deviations, meaning the models' recall distributions barely overlap across folds. This is the same logic Chapter 13's cross-validation chapter uses to distinguish a genuine model-selection signal from noise: look at the spread, not just the point estimate, before trusting a comparison.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 37.5's two measured PSI values (0.4704 for the drifted batch, 0.0482 for the no-drift control), explain why testing the monitoring check against BOTH a genuinely-drifted batch and a no-drift control batch is necessary to trust the check. What would a single PSI value, with nothing to compare it against, fail to demonstrate?
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A single PSI value with nothing to compare it against can't distinguish "the check is working correctly and detected a real shift" from "the check always reports a high number regardless of input," or conversely "the check never reports a high number regardless of input." Either failure mode would look identical to a correctly-functioning check if only one batch were ever tested. Testing against both a genuinely-drifted batch (0.4704, correctly flagged as major) and a no-drift control batch drawn from the same distribution as training (0.0482, correctly not flagged) demonstrates the check discriminates in both directions. It doesn't just always fire, and it doesn't just never fire. That's the minimum evidence needed to trust it as a real monitoring signal rather than a check that happens to look plausible.

bookExercises.prompt: A colleague's capstone trains five different model architectures, tunes each extensively, and reports the best cross-validated F1 score, with no deployment code and no monitoring check. Using this chapter's rubric-style Trade-offs framing, write the two or three sentences you'd say about what's missing.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "Five tuned architectures and a strong CV F1 score demonstrate real modelling skill, but per this chapter's rubric, that's only one dimension of a capstone. Modelling is often over-invested in relative to its real payoff (Procedure 37.2's effort allocation caps it at 25%), while deployment and monitoring, entirely missing here, are worth 30% combined and are the stages that prove the model could actually be used, not just scored. A modest single model with real deployment and monitoring code demonstrates more of this book's stated goal than five well-tuned models that only exist as notebook cells."

bookExercises.prompt: This chapter's Worked Example chose Logistic Regression over Random Forest specifically because of the failure-cost asymmetry in a predictive-maintenance problem. Describe a different business problem (naming it explicitly) where the same measured recall gap would justify the opposite choice: accepting far more missed positives in exchange for far fewer false alarms.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Fraud/anomaly detection on financial transactions: here, a false positive (flagging a legitimate transaction as fraud) has a real cost, blocked legitimate purchases, customer friction, support burden, while a missed fraud case, though costly, is often one of many transactions and may be partially recoverable through other controls (chargebacks, insurance). A model tuned to minimize false alarms even at the cost of missing more fraud cases could be the right choice if the business's actual cost structure makes "don't annoy legitimate customers" the dominant concern: the opposite trade-off from this chapter's predictive-maintenance example, where a missed failure (unplanned downtime, safety risk) dominates the cost of an extra inspection.

bookExercises.prompt: Read Chapter 21's discussion of governance and fairness considerations. For the predictive-maintenance Worked Example in this chapter, identify one plausible fairness-adjacent question worth naming even if ultimately out of scope for a solo capstone (per Procedure 37.1's "Out of Scope" field), and explain why naming it explicitly is better practice than omitting it silently.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A plausible fairness-adjacent question: if `runtime_hours` or maintenance history correlates with which facility or region a pump is deployed in, a model trained to prioritize inspection resources based on predicted failure risk could systematically under-prioritize maintenance in facilities with less complete sensor logging (more missing `vibration` readings) purely due to data quality differences rather than genuine risk differences, effectively deprioritizing maintenance where monitoring infrastructure is already weakest. Naming this explicitly in the "Out of Scope" section, even without solving it, is better practice than silent omission, because it tells a future reader (or the practitioner's future self) that the question was considered and consciously deferred, rather than leaving it ambiguous whether it was missed entirely. That's the same distinction Chapter 21's governance chapter draws between an unexamined blind spot and a documented, deliberate scope boundary.
